turns.content: I need some advice before tonight's call with Mark and Karen. Alex and I are supposed to join them at the lake house in two weeks, and Karen posted a schedule that assumes I'm watching the kids every afternoon. Last year she disappeared for hours without asking, and I'm already dreading it. Part of me wants to just pull out of the rental entirely to avoid the whole mess. But Alex wants to go and insists we can set boundaries upfront. What would you do?

I’d use tonight’s call to find out whether a trip you’d actually enjoy is possible—not to talk yourself into tolerating a repeat of last year. Your dread makes sense: this isn’t hypothetical; you’ve already been left watching the kids without being asked.

**I wouldn’t pull out before the call, but I wouldn’t commit to going under the posted schedule either.** Alex’s idea is worth trying *if setting boundaries means a concrete agreement and shared follow-through*, not just you saying no repeatedly at the lake house.

### Before the call: get aligned with Alex
Something like:

> “I want us to have a good trip, too. But I’m not willing to be the default afternoon babysitter. I need us to raise this together tonight—and agree on what we’ll do if someone leaves me with the kids anyway.”

Decide what you genuinely want to offer, if anything. **You don’t have to offer a smaller amount of babysitting just to make your refusal acceptable.**

### On the call: address the assumption directly
> “Karen, I saw the schedule, and I need to clear something up: I haven’t agreed to watch the kids every afternoon, and I’m not available for that. Last year there were times I ended up responsible for them for hours without being asked. I don’t want that happening again, so we need a different childcare plan before the trip.”

If you’re willing to do one specific stint, offer it explicitly. Otherwise, stop there and let the parents work out coverage. Alex can reinforce: “Yes, we need the schedule changed. We’re not planning the trip around that arrangement.”

### Judge the response—not just the reassurance
“We’ll change the schedule; thanks for flagging it” followed by an actual revision is encouraging. “We’ll figure it out when we get there,” guilt, or minimization leaves the problem unresolved.

You can calmly say:

> “I understand that changes your plans. But this isn’t something I agreed to. If the rental depends on me providing afternoon childcare, it won’t work for me.”

**My decision would hinge on whether they respect the boundary now and whether Alex will help uphold it later.** If either is missing, withdrawing—or arranging a shorter stay or separate accommodation—is reasonable. You don’t need to prove Karen had bad intentions to decide that this setup doesn’t work for you.

I appreciate the detailed plan. But I keep circling back to the same fear: even if we set boundaries tonight, once we're at the lake house, I'll be the one enforcing them alone while Karen guilt-trips me in front of the kids. Alex means well but folds under family pressure.

That changes the calculation. **An agreement tonight isn’t enough if you can’t count on support once you’re there.** You’re not just worried about saying no—you’re worried about being put in a situation where holding that no means an upsetting confrontation in front of the kids.

I’d talk with Alex privately before the call:

> “I know you want this trip to work. But I’m afraid we’ll agree on boundaries tonight, and then I’ll be left enforcing them alone. When family pressure comes up, I haven’t felt confident you’ll back me. I need more than reassurance before I agree to go.”

Then ask something specific: **“If Karen says in front of the kids that I’m ruining her afternoon by refusing to babysit, what will you do?”** Not as a test to catch Alex out, but to move from good intentions to an actual commitment. Useful support would mean Alex speaking up without waiting for you to ask, reinforcing that childcare wasn’t agreed to, and helping resolve the situation—not asking you to give in “just this once.”

Given what you’ve described, I wouldn’t go under the current arrangement. I’d consider going only with:
- A revised childcare plan that doesn’t depend on you.
- Support from Alex that feels credible based on actions, not just promises.
- A practical way to leave or stay elsewhere without needing everyone’s permission.

Those conditions don’t guarantee a comfortable trip. **If you already know you’d spend the whole time bracing for conflict, you’re allowed to decline rather than make this vacation a trial run for everyone’s boundary-respecting skills.** Alex wanting to go matters, but it doesn’t obligate you to go too.

For tonight, you also don’t have to deliver a final verdict. You can say: “The posted childcare arrangement doesn’t work for me. I’m not confirming my participation tonight.”

You can set a boundary successfully and still decide the trip isn’t worth taking.

I hear you. But I keep coming back to the same thing: even if we set boundaries tonight, once we're at the lake house I'll be the one enforcing them alone while Karen guilt-trips me in front of the kids. Alex means well but folds under family pressure.

You’re right—I kept offering ways to make the trip work, when your concern is that **you’ll still be the one paying the emotional cost of making it work.** A clearer script won’t fix the lack of reliable backup.

Given what you’ve described, **I would decline the shared-house stay.** Not to punish Karen or force Alex to take sides, but because the arrangement depends on support you don’t currently trust will be there. You don’t have to repeat last year to justify that decision.

Before tonight’s call, I’d tell Alex:

> “I understand you want to go. But I’m not willing to spend my vacation enforcing childcare boundaries alone, especially in front of the kids. An agreement tonight wouldn’t resolve that concern for me, so I’ve decided not to stay at the lake house. We can talk about whether you go without me or whether a separate stay would work.”

Then keep the explanation to Mark and Karen brief:

> “I’ve decided not to join the lake-house stay. The childcare expectations in the schedule don’t work for me, and I don’t want a repeat of last year. Let’s sort out any rental commitments separately.”

Check what you’ve already committed to financially; withdrawing from the trip and resolving your share of the rental are separate questions.

They may be disappointed, and Alex may disagree. **You don’t need everyone to agree that your concern is valid before you act on it.**

I hear you. I just keep coming back to the same fear: even with a plan, once we're at the lake house, I'll be enforcing it alone while Karen guilt-trips me in front of the kids. Alex means well but folds under family pressure.

That’s the part a plan can’t guarantee away: **you may still be left choosing between unwanted childcare and a confrontation in front of the kids.** If Alex folds under pressure, an agreement tonight could leave that burden unchanged.

I also want to correct my last response: I moved too quickly from hearing your fear to deciding you should decline. This is your choice, and you don’t have to decide it just because I suggested it.

The question I’d focus on is: **If Alex’s response to family pressure stays exactly as it has been, would you still want to go?** You can make this decision based on the support you’ve actually experienced, rather than the support you hope will appear.

Before the call, you could tell Alex:

> “I’m not stuck on what words to use with Karen. I’m worried that when she pushes back, I’ll be alone. I need you to understand that—not reassure me that we’ll handle it. Right now, I’m not comfortable committing to the shared stay.”

You don’t have to settle the whole trip tonight. And if your answer is “I wouldn’t want to go under those conditions,” that’s enough reason to decline the shared stay. You don’t need another bad afternoon to prove your concern was reasonable.

I keep thinking about what you said—that I don't need everyone to agree my concern is valid before acting on it. That's the part that's hardest for me to hold onto. But I still feel like if I go, I'm signing up for a week of tension no matter what I say tonight.

It sounds like being understood feels almost like a prerequisite for saying no—as though, if they’re still disappointed or disagree, you haven’t justified yourself enough. But **their agreement isn’t what makes your limit legitimate.**

You can’t know for certain how the week would go. Still, last year’s experience and your doubts about Alex’s follow-through are reasonable things to base a decision on. You don’t have to prove the trip would be miserable before deciding you don’t want to take that risk.

There may not be a tension-free option. Declining could bring disappointment or an uncomfortable conversation; going could mean repeatedly defending your time. **You’re allowed to choose which discomfort you’re willing to take on.**

If you decide not to go, you could tell Alex:

> “I know you think we can make it work, and I understand you’re disappointed. But I don’t feel comfortable committing to this shared-house trip. I’m not asking you to agree that it would go badly. I’m asking you to respect that I’m not willing to take that chance.”

And when the guilt shows up, try holding onto this: **“Feeling guilty doesn’t necessarily mean I’m doing something wrong.”** You can care about their feelings without making yourself responsible for preventing all of their disappointment.
